title: Galvanised Z275 Steel Water Tanks in South Africa: What the Zinc Coating Can and Cannot Do
excerpt: A practical engineering guide to galvanised steel water tanks in South Africa: what Z275 means, how zinc protects steel, and where it falls short.
content:
Galvanised steel water tanks are the most common steel storage option on South African farms, lodges and industrial sites. Most buyers see "galvanised" and assume decades of rust-free service. The truth is more useful than that. A galvanised coating does excellent work in the right conditions and fails quickly in the wrong ones.

This guide explains what a Z275 galvanised coating actually is, how zinc protects steel, and how it behaves in South African water. It covers hard borehole water, soft Western Cape supply, acidic rainwater and coastal air. It also explains why the liner, not the zinc, usually decides how long a tank lasts.

What "Z275" means on a galvanised steel water tank

The "Z" grades describe continuously galvanised steel sheet. Steel coil runs through a molten zinc bath at the mill and comes out with a thin zinc layer on both faces. The number is the total coating mass on both faces, in grams per square metre.

That detail matters. Z275, the grade Damtech uses for its galvanised tanks, does not mean 275 g/m² on each side. It means roughly 137.5 g/m² of zinc per face, which works out to about 19.3 µm per face at nominal thickness. The lighter Z250 grade, common in the market, gives about 17.5 µm.

Grade Total coating, both faces (g/m²) Nominal thickness per face (µm) Zinc per face (g/m²)
Z275 275 19.3 137.5
Z250 250 17.5 125

Figures derived from coating mass and the density of zinc (7.14 g/cm³), as set out in GalvInfoNote 1.1.

Two further points catch buyers out:

  • One face is usually thinner. Coating mass is measured as an average across both faces. For Z275, the thinner face is around 13 to 14 µm (GalvInfoNote 1.1). Inside a tank, that thinner face may be the one holding water.
  • Grades vary by standard. Z275 appears in EN 10346 grade lists, while Z250 is missing from at least one of them. Whatever you buy, ask for the mill certificate and check the standard and designation it states.

Sheet, not plate, and not batch galvanising

Z275 is a coil-coated sheet product, normally in light gauges. It is not structural plate. It is also different from batch hot-dip galvanising, where a finished, fabricated item is dipped after forming.

Batch galvanising builds zinc-iron alloy layers usually 55 to over 100 µm thick (HDGASA Info Sheet 6). That is roughly three to five times the zinc on one face of Z275. Batch work falls under SANS 121 / ISO 1461. ISO 1461:2022 expressly excludes continuously galvanised sheet, so a "SANS 121 compliant" claim on a Z275 sheet tank is the wrong reference.

This is why long-life stories about old pressed-steel tanks do not transfer to thin sheet. Those tanks were usually batch galvanised with far more zinc.

How zinc protects a steel water tank

Zinc protects steel in two ways.

  1. Sacrificial (cathodic) protection. Zinc is more reactive than steel. Where the coating is scratched or cut, the zinc corrodes first and protects the exposed steel nearby.
  2. A protective surface film. In the right water, zinc forms a carbonate-based film that slows further corrosion. Hardness and alkalinity in the water support this film.

The second mechanism is the important one inside a tank. Zinc's corrosion rate in water depends heavily on water chemistry. In hard, scale-forming water the film can almost stop corrosion. In soft, low-alkalinity water the film struggles to form, and zinc is consumed much faster.

Continuous immersion vs fluctuating water levels

Fully submerged walls

Industry tables give typical zinc loss rates for fresh water. The table below shows how long one wetted face of Z275 would last if those rates were sustained.

Water type Typical zinc loss (µm/year) Z275 face, 19.3 µm (years) Batch galvanised, 85 µm (years)
Hard fresh water 2.5–5 3.9–7.7 17–34
Soft fresh water 5–10 1.9–3.9 8.5–17

Rates from the GAA/GANZ durability guide. Years are simple division and indicate scale only.

Read this table as an order of magnitude, not a service-life promise. Two effects pull in opposite directions. Scale can slow zinc far below these rates in hard water. But pits, cut edges and the thinner face fail ahead of the average.

The message is still clear. About 19 µm of zinc is a thin reserve for a wetted surface.

The waterline band

Many farm tanks cycle between full and half-full. That creates a band of wall that is wet, then dry, then wet again.

The evidence here is thin. In seawater, zinc in tidal and splash zones typically corrodes about twice as fast as fully immersed zinc (HDGASA Info Sheet 3). The American Galvanizers Association adds that agitation accelerates waterline attack in fresh and sea water (AGA).

No fresh-water waterline test or tank teardown was found. A static waterline with sediment or biofilm is a likely weak point, but that is an engineering inference, not a measurement.

The headspace under the roof

The air gap above the water is humid and poorly ventilated. On zinc, trapped moisture produces loose white rust (GalvInfoNote 3.3). Condensate is also soft water, even when the stored water is hard. No tank-headspace study was found, so treat the roof underside as a wet, not an atmospheric, surface.

Galvanised tanks and South African water

South Africa's water varies sharply by source and region. That variation matters more for a galvanised tank than the coating grade does.

South African water What it does to zinc Practical reading
Soft, low-alkalinity supply Zinc is prone to severe attack below 50 mg/L as CaCO₃ (HDGASA) Worst realistic case. Line the tank
Hard, scale-forming borehole water Scale can virtually stop corrosion at pH 6 to 8 Zinc's best case
Chlorinated municipal water Chlorine at drinking levels is not a proven driver Low alkalinity is the real risk
Rainwater Highveld rain measured at pH 4.65 to 4.80, below zinc's stated lower limit of about pH 5.5 to 6 Line the tank

The Western Cape is a soft-water region. Every City of Cape Town supply reported for January to March 2026 fell below the 50 mg/L line. Hardness ranged from 16 to 46 mg/L and alkalinity from 8 to 26 mg/L as CaCO₃ (City of Cape Town). Bare zinc in that water is in its least favourable class.

Rainwater harvesting tanks face the same problem. Rain lacks the dissolved salts that build zinc's protective film. Highveld rain readings come from Water SA. Contact with roof dust and the tank itself will raise the pH in storage somewhat, but not enough to rely on.

Hard borehole water can be zinc's friend. If a laboratory analysis shows scale-forming chemistry, bare zinc has a documented protective mechanism. Get the analysis before relying on it. Hardness, alkalinity, pH, chloride, sulphate and copper are the minimum.

Copper deserves a special warning. About 0.1 ppm of dissolved copper is named as enough to cause rapid pitting of zinc (GAA). Keep copper pipe and fittings out of, and upstream of, a galvanised tank.

Positives and engineering advantages of galvanised Z275

  • More sacrificial zinc than Aluzinc at a similar thickness. Z275 carries about 4.2 times the zinc per face of AZ150 Aluzinc. Zinc is the metal that does the sacrificial work. See Aluzinc water storage tanks for the detail.
  • A documented mechanism in water. Zinc is the only one of the two coatings with a described self-protecting film in fresh water, provided the water is hard and scale-forming.
  • Better short-term cut-edge behaviour. Cleveland-Cliffs, which sells both products, says galvanised may show less cut-edge red rust than aluminium-zinc in the short term, under about 10 years depending on environment (product data).
  • Tolerates cured concrete. Galvanising embedded in sound concrete is reported to corrode below 0.1 µm/year. That makes zinc the more forgiving coating where a tank bears on a cured, separated plinth.
  • Forms well. Zinc coatings adhere well through tight bends and corrugations, which suits roll-formed tank sheets.
  • Familiar repairs. Zinc-rich repair systems are established and widely available.

Negatives and environmental limitations

Coastal and industrial air (ISO 9223 C3 to C5)

The outside face of a tank lives in the atmosphere. Corrosivity is classed from C1 (very low) to CX (extreme). Using ISO 9224 long-term zinc rates, a Z275 face at nominal thickness gives these planning lines:

Atmosphere Z275 planning line (years) Published Z275 range (years)
C3 (medium, most inland and many coastal-hinterland sites) about 18 12–42
C4 (high) about 9 5–12
C5 (very high) about 4 2–5

Planning lines are derived from the top of the ISO 9224 steady-state zinc rates. The ranges are published for Z275 in the GAA/GANZ guide. Multiply by about 0.7 for the thinner face.

South Africa's peer-reviewed corrosion map shows how fast the class rises near the sea. The first 150 m from the shore is CX, and 150 to 1,000 m sits in mid-C4 to mid-C5 (Janse van Rensburg et al., 2019). Sites 1 to 30 km inland are largely C3. Those classes were measured on steel, so a site's zinc class should be checked, not assumed.

For a tank within a kilometre of the sea, bare Z275 on the outside is a short-life coating. Paint, duplex systems or a different coating are worth pricing.

Soft water, acidic water and the inside face

As above, soft water and rainwater are zinc's worst cases. A bare Z275 tank in Cape Town supply or on a rainwater system should be treated as a consumable, not a long-term asset.

Drinking water

SANS 241-1:2015 sets an aesthetic limit for zinc of 5 mg/L. Australian guidance reports legacy galvanised rainwater tanks typically at 2 to 4 mg/L zinc, and up to 11 mg/L (NHMRC). No potable-water certification for a bare galvanised sheet surface was found. For drinking water, specify a wetted surface with its own evidence.

Specifications and the DWS 9900 benchmark

The Department of Water and Sanitation's DWS 9900 corrosion protection specification is written mainly for pipelines and galvanised articles. It does not name Z275 or tank sheet, and it binds only where a contract invokes it. Its galvanising chapter still sets the benchmark a reviewing engineer is likely to use:

  • Heavy-duty galvanising starts at 55 µm for steel below 1.5 mm. Z275's 19.3 µm per face is about 35% of that.
  • Galvanised structures are not to be subjected to stagnant water, on oxygen-depletion grounds.
  • A water analysis goes to the corrosion engineer, who decides whether an internal polymer lining or overcoat is needed.

So DWS 9900 does not ban galvanised steel in water. It does expect a lining decision based on the water.

International bolted tanks are covered by ANSI/AWWA D103, which addresses factory-coated bolted steel tanks. A light-gauge corrugated farm tank is a different product class.

Where a galvanised steel water tank makes sense

The research points to one clear rule. Specify the water barrier first and the metallic coating second.

  • Lined galvanised tank. The liner carries the water duty, and the zinc protects the shell from the outside air and from incidental moisture. This is the configuration Damtech supplies: its corrugated galvanised tanks come with a 550 gsm PVC liner (850 gsm on request) and a bidim floor sheet, over a Z275 galvanised shell. Damtech also supplies AZ150 Aluzinc tanks with the same liner.
  • Unlined galvanised tank in hard water. Defensible only with a water analysis showing scale-forming chemistry, the heaviest available coating, and an owner who accepts a finite life with inspections.
  • Unlined galvanised tank in soft or acidic water. Not recommended. Line it.

For long-life unlined steel, the stronger route is batch galvanising at heavy-duty thickness or a certified factory coating, not thin sheet.

What galvanised steel water tanks cost in South Africa

There is no reliable published price bracket for Z275 tanks across the South African market. Prices depend on diameter, height, sheet gauge, coating grade (Z275 galvanised or Aluzinc), liner, roof, fittings, transport and installation. Commercial and industrial tanks are priced to a specification.

For reference, Damtech's current supply-only kit prices, including VAT, PVC liner and standard fittings, are:

Damtech kit Size (diameter × height) Price incl. VAT
10 000 L water tank 3 m × 1.5 m R13 999
20 000 L water tank 4 m × 1.5 m R18 999
50 000 L water tank 5 m × 2.3 m R31 999
100 000 L water tank 9 m × 1.5 m R43 999

Delivery, base preparation and installation are excluded and quoted separately. Larger reservoirs, from about 11 kL to 500 kL and beyond, are quoted per project on the steel water storage tanks page.

When comparing quotes, ask each supplier for the coating grade per face, the mill certificate, the liner thickness and what is excluded. A cheaper tank with a thinner coating and no liner is not a like-for-like price.

Key takeaways

  • Z275 means about 19.3 µm of zinc per face, not 275 g/m² per side.
  • Zinc protects well in hard, scale-forming water and poorly in soft, acidic or rain water.
  • On the outside, bare Z275 is a short-life coating within about 1 km of the coast.
  • A qualified liner is what makes a galvanised steel water tank last.

For the full side-by-side picture, read Aluzinc vs galvanised steel water tanks. If you are buying storage ahead of a dry summer, see El Niño 2026/27 and water security on South African farms.

title: El Niño 2026/27: What It Means for Water Security on South African Farms
excerpt: A very strong El Niño is under way. See what SAWS forecasts, where South African farms are most exposed and how to secure farm water before summer peaks.
content:
South Africa is heading into one of the strongest El Niño events on record, and the water risk it brings is very different from one farm to the next. National dams are close to full, yet many farms still depend on a single borehole, a small earth dam or a few tanks. This guide pulls together the latest forecasts and what they mean for water security on South African farms in the 2026/27 season.

Forecasts describe probabilities, not certainties, so treat this as a planning guide and check the latest outlooks from the South African Weather Service (SAWS) as the season unfolds.

What is El Niño, and how strong is this one?

El Niño is a warming of the central and eastern Pacific Ocean that shifts weather patterns around the world. Over southern Africa it tends to bring lower summer rainfall and higher temperatures, although the effect varies from season to season.

NOAA's Climate Prediction Center issued an El Niño Advisory in June 2026 and put the chance of a "very strong" event at about 63%. On 1 September SAWS said Pacific sea-surface temperatures had already crossed the very-strong threshold and that the event could become the strongest in living memory, peaking between about October 2026 and January 2027 (SAnews).

What the forecasts say for South African farmers

  • Below-normal rainfall is favoured over most of the country for October to December 2026, and November to January looks very similar.
  • Above-normal temperatures are considered very likely, with heatwaves more frequent if the dry conditions materialise.
  • The far north-east, including the Kruger National Park area, is expected to be hardest hit, and KwaZulu-Natal can expect El Niño effects from October 2026 to March 2027.
  • The event is not expected to fade until around February or March 2027, close to the end of the summer cropping season.

SAWS has also cautioned that a strong El Niño does not automatically mean severe drought. Of the three very strong events since 1979, 1982/83 and 2015/16 brought widespread drought, but 1997/98 brought slightly above-normal rain to parts of the summer rainfall region. Its advice is simple: manage conservatively and prepare early.

Why full dams do not mean every farm is safe

South Africa enters the season in a much stronger position than in 2015. National dam storage was about 95.6% on 2 November 2026, compared with about 55% in August 2016, according to the Department of Water and Sanitation's weekly reservoir report. Soil moisture and veld are also in good condition after a long, wet 2025/26 season.

That protects bulk supply and irrigation schemes, but it leaves real gaps:

  • About 80% of field crops are rain-fed. Full dams do little for dryland maize or grazing when summer rain fails.
  • The Western Cape had one of its driest winters in decades. Its main supply system was around 79% in September, with several key dams far below last year, and agricultural allocations are at risk if the next winter is also dry.
  • Boreholes and small farm dams react fast. In 2015/16, 29 of 89 emergency boreholes drilled came up dry, which shows that groundwater is not an automatic fallback in a deep drought.
  • Municipal systems lose a large share of water to leaks. National non-revenue water is about 47%, so outages can happen even when dams are full.

In other words, the most useful question for a farmer is not "are the dams full?" but "how much water do I have stored, and how much of it will I lose before I use it?"

Where farm water is most exposed this summer

RegionMain water exposure
Limpopo and MpumalangaRain-fed crops, cattle, communal grazing and heat stress on subtropical fruit
Free State and North WestDryland maize and sunflower; livestock grazing. Dams are full, but rain-fed land is exposed
KwaZulu-NatalSugarcane, veld-fire risk and municipal water losses
Eastern CapeLivestock, which suffered heavy losses in 2015/16
Western CapeLow dam levels after a dry winter and possible allocation cuts

These ratings are a qualitative summary of the research, not an official classification.

Lessons from the 2015/16 drought

The last very strong El Niño left a clear record. About 246,600 farmers were affected and roughly 186,000 livestock died. Researchers warned that the loss of breeding stock would cause livestock shortages for two to four years afterwards (Scholtz et al., 2016). Relief arrived late: by March 2016 only about 42,000 farmers had been assisted (SAnews).

The practical lesson is that the farms that coped best were those that had secured water and feed before the dry spell hit.

Practical steps to secure farm water now

  1. Find and fix leaks. A dam or reservoir that loses water through seepage or a failed liner is losing your drought reserve. Our guide to diagnosing farm dam leaks shows what to look for, and our dam repair service can assess a leaking dam on site.
  2. Line unlined or failing dams. Dam linings such as HDPE reduce seepage losses so more of the water you capture stays available.
  3. Add storage you control. Tanks and reservoirs next to your borehole or dam give you a buffer. See our corrugated steel water storage tanks and our agricultural water storage solutions.
  4. Add water points for livestock. The Department of Agriculture advises increasing the number of water and feed points, so check your troughs, pumps and pipelines before the heat arrives.
  5. Plan your levels. Our guide on managing farm dam water levels during prolonged droughts covers how to stretch what you have.
  6. Size your storage properly. Use our water storage calculators to estimate lining area and tank size before you ask for a quote.

What to watch over the coming months

  • Monthly: the SAWS seasonal outlook and NOAA's ENSO update.
  • Weekly: DWS reservoir reports for your catchment, plus your own dam and borehole levels.
  • Late January to February 2027: rainfall and heat during maize flowering, the most critical yield window.

Frequently asked questions

Will El Niño cause a drought in South Africa in 2026/27?

Below-normal rainfall is favoured, but it is not guaranteed. Impacts will depend on local rainfall and other climate drivers. Because a very strong El Niño has brought both severe drought and near-normal rain in the past, preparing for a dry summer is the safer plan.

Are South African dams full going into El Niño?

Nationally, yes: storage was about 95.6% in early November 2026. The Western Cape is lower, at around 79%, and farms that rely on boreholes, rainfall or small private dams are not protected by national dam levels.

What is the best way for a farmer to prepare for El Niño?

Secure and protect your own water: repair leaks, line dams that lose water, add storage and water points, and match livestock numbers to your grazing and water supply.

title: Leaking Farm Dam? How to Find the Leak and Fix It
excerpt: How to tell if a farm dam is leaking, find where the water goes, judge how serious it is and choose the right repair.
content:
Is your farm dam leaking? If the water drops when nobody is using it, and faster than the sun and wind can explain, it probably is. First confirm the leak with a simple bucket test. Then walk the dam to find where the water goes, judge how serious it is, and pick a repair that suits your dam.

This guide covers lined and unlined earth dams. For steel tanks, see our guide to fixing a leaking steel water tank.

Quick answer: leaking farm dam signs and what to do

SignWhat it usually meansWhat to do
Level drops with no pumping or rainA leak, seepage or a hidden pipe lossDo the bucket test below
Wet or very green patch below the wallWater seeping through the wall or floorMark it and watch if it grows
Muddy water flowing out below the wallSoil washing out of the wallStop using the dam and call an engineer now
Tear, hole or loose edge in the linerLiner damage, often at the waterlinePatch or replace that part of the liner
Wet ground at a valve or pipePipe or fitting leakRepair the fitting; often a quick fix

How do I know if my farm dam is leaking?

Every open dam loses some water to evaporation. The bucket test tells you if it loses more than that.

  1. Put a bucket on a step or block in the shallow water, so its rim sits above the dam water.
  2. Fill the bucket with dam water to the same level as the dam.
  3. Mark the water level inside the bucket and on a stake in the dam.
  4. Wait two or three days. Do not pump from the dam, and start again if it rains.
  5. Compare the two drops.

If both levels dropped by the same amount, the loss is evaporation. If the dam dropped more than the bucket, the dam is losing water another way: a leak, seepage or a pipe.

Where is the water going?

Walk the whole dam, not only the water. Check these places in this order:

  • Pipes and valves. Look for wet ground along the outlet pipe and at every valve and trough. A leaking pipe is often blamed on the dam.
  • The waterline. On a lined dam, look for tears, holes and creases where the water meets the liner. Sun, animals and floating branches do most damage here.
  • Seams and the anchor trench. Check that welded seams are closed and that the liner edge is still buried at the top of the bank.
  • Below the wall. Look for wet ground, springs, reeds or very green grass at the bottom of the outside slope (the toe).
  • The floor of an unlined dam. Sandy and gravel soils let water seep straight down. You will not see this, but the bucket test shows it.

Tip: put a little food colouring or non-toxic dye in the water near a suspected hole. If it gets pulled into a gap, you have found the leak.

Is the leak serious?

LevelWhat you seeAction
SmallOne tear or a leaking fitting; the wall is dry and firmPlan a repair soon
GrowingSeveral tears, brittle or cracked liner, liner sliding down the bankGet the liner assessed; a partial or full reline may be cheaper than many patches
DangerousSoft, slumping or cracked wall, or muddy water flowing out below itStop using the dam, lower the water if it is safe to, keep people and animals away, and get an engineer

Muddy seepage means the water is carrying soil out of the wall. That hole can grow fast from the inside. It is not a patching job.

How do you fix a leaking farm dam?

The right repair depends on what the dam is made of and how big the damage is.

RepairSuitsLimits
Liner patchSmall tears in HDPE or PVC liner that is still in good conditionHDPE patches must be welded by a trained welder; the area must be clean and dry
Partial or full relineOld, brittle or widely damaged liner, or an unlined dam that seepsThe basin must be drained and shaped first
Torch-on bitumenCracked concrete or cement dams and wallsNeeds a sound, dry surface and a skilled applicator
Clay or bentonite sealingSome unlined earth damsLess reliable on sandy soil or soil that moves
Pipe and valve repairLeaks at fittings, outlets and troughsFix the cause, such as a stuck float valve

If you need help, our leaking dam repair team can assess the dam and tell you which repair makes sense.

Can I fix a dam leak myself?

You can fix most pipe, valve and trough leaks yourself. A small PVC patch with the supplier's repair kit can also work above the waterline.

HDPE needs hot-wedge or extrusion welding, so a patch needs the right machine and a trained welder. Any problem with the wall itself needs an engineer, not a patch.

How to stop new leaks

  • Check the waterline, seams and toe once a month and after big storms.
  • Fence the dam and give animals a trough or a protected drinking point.
  • Keep trees and reeds away from the liner. See vegetation control around lined dams.
  • Read how to stop a dam liner failing early.

Frequently asked questions

How do I know if my farm dam is leaking?

Do the bucket test. Set a bucket of dam water in the dam for two or three days without pumping. If the dam drops more than the bucket, it is losing water to more than evaporation.

Why is my dam losing water when nobody uses it?

The usual causes are evaporation, seepage through the floor or wall, a liner tear, or a leaking pipe or trough. Our guide to why a farm dam loses water explains how to tell them apart.

What does a wet patch below a dam wall mean?

Water is getting through the wall or under it. Clear water that stays the same size needs watching and a repair plan. Muddy water, or a patch that grows, needs an engineer straight away.

Can a leaking dam liner be patched?

Yes, if the rest of the liner is still in good condition. If the liner is brittle or has many tears, a reline usually works out better than repeated patches.

Do I have to drain the dam to fix a leak?

Not always. Repairs above the waterline can often be done with water in the dam. Leaks lower down usually need the water lowered so the liner is clean and dry.

title: Farm Dam Maintenance: How to Stop Your Dam Liner Failing
excerpt: The five places a farm dam liner usually fails, a simple monthly and yearly maintenance checklist, and when a repair needs a specialist.
content:
How do you stop a farm dam liner from failing? Walk the dam regularly, look at the five places where liners usually fail, and fix small damage before it grows. Most liner failures start at the edge, the waterline, a pipe, a stone underneath or where animals walk in. A short monthly check and a closer yearly inspection catch nearly all of them early.

Quick answer: farm dam maintenance

How oftenWhat to do
Every monthWalk the crest. Check the liner edge, the waterline and the pipes. Look for wet patches outside the dam.
After a stormCheck the anchor trench, loose edges, washed-out banks and fallen branches.
Once a yearInspect the whole liner when the water is low. Check seams, patches, fences and drainage.
Straight awayRepair any hole, tear or lifted edge before the dam fills again.

Where do farm dam liners fail?

Liners rarely fail in the middle of a clean sheet. They fail at weak points. The drawing shows the five most common ones.

  1. The edge at the crest. If the anchor trench is shallow or washes out, wind gets under the liner and lifts it. A flapping edge tears quickly.
  2. The waterline. The band where the water level rises and falls gets the most sun, heat and wave action. Floating debris also rubs here.
  3. Pipes through the bank. Inlets, outlets and overflows need a sealed boot where they pass through the liner. Poorly sealed pipes are a common leak.
  4. Stones under the floor. A stone or root left under the liner is pushed up by the weight of the water until it wears through.
  5. Livestock and machinery. Hooves, tractor wheels and dragged pipes cut and scuff the liner, mostly on the slopes.

Your monthly dam check

A monthly walk around the dam takes less than half an hour. Take a phone and photograph anything that changes.

  • Edge: is the liner still buried in the anchor trench all the way round? Any lifted or flapping sections?
  • Waterline: any cracks, scuffs, wrinkles or debris caught against the liner?
  • Pipes: any drips or wet ground at the inlet, outlet and overflow?
  • Outside the dam: any wet patches, green grass or seepage at the foot of the bank? That often means a leak.
  • Water level: is it dropping faster than you would expect from use and evaporation?
  • Fences: are livestock kept off the liner?

If the level drops for no clear reason, follow our guide to finding a leak in a farm dam.

Your yearly dam inspection

Once a year, ideally when the water is low, look at the whole liner more closely.

CheckWhat to look for
SeamsLifting, open or peeling joints
Old patchesEdges coming loose
FloorBumps from stones, soft spots, sediment build-up
SlopesScuffs, cuts, hoof marks, bulges from water or gas underneath
Banks and trenchErosion, animal burrows, cracks in the crest
Around the damTrees and reeds growing too close

Plants near the dam are a slow but real risk. Our guide to weeds and trees around a lined dam explains what to remove.

Simple habits that stop damage

  • Fence the dam and give livestock a trough or a protected drinking point instead.
  • Do not drive on the liner or drag pipes, pumps or tools across it.
  • Keep the crest clear so you can see the edge and the trench.
  • Clear sediment carefully with soft tools or a pump, never with a bucket or blade on the liner.
  • Do not let the dam stand empty for long in high wind. An empty liner is light and easy to lift.

When to call a specialist

Small, clean holes can be patched quickly by a trained installer. Call in a repair team when you see any of these:

  • A tear longer than your hand, or many holes in one area
  • Seams that have opened
  • A leak at a pipe that you cannot see clearly
  • Large sections of liner lifted by wind
  • A liner that has gone brittle or cracked in many places

Patching HDPE needs an extrusion welder, and patching PVC needs the right method for that material. Tape and glue from a hardware shop rarely last on a dam liner.

Frequently asked questions

How often should a farm dam be inspected?

Walk the dam once a month and after every big storm. Do a full inspection of the liner once a year, when the water is low.

What is the most common cause of dam liner failure?

Poor preparation under the liner and damage at the edges. Stones under the sheet, loose anchor trenches and livestock on the slopes are among the most common causes.

Can I repair a dam liner myself?

Small tears can be patched, but the patch must be the same material and welded or bonded properly. A badly made patch often leaks again within months.

Does a lined dam need maintenance at all?

Yes. A liner needs far less work than an unlined earth dam, but it still needs regular checks, a clear edge and protection from animals.

Need a liner repaired?

title: Leaking Steel Water Tank: How to Find the Leak and Fix It
excerpt: A step-by-step guide to finding a leak in a lined corrugated steel water tank, with the usual causes and the right repair for each.
content:
Why is my steel water tank leaking? In a lined corrugated steel tank, the steel does not hold the water. The PVC liner does. So most leaks come from a hole or split in the liner, a failed seam at the floor, or a leaking outlet or valve. Rust on the steel is a problem for the structure, but it is rarely where the water escapes.

This guide helps you find the leak, work out the cause and choose the right repair.

Quick answer: what the signs mean

What you seeLikely causeWhat to do
The level drops and the ground is wet round the baseHole in the liner or a split floor seamFind the height of the leak, then patch or reline
A wet patch under the outletOutlet fitting, seal or valveReseal or replace the fitting
Water runs from the overflow or over the topFloat valve stuck openFix the float valve; this is not a leak
Rust streaks or holes in a panelCorrosion of the steelTreat surface rust; replace a holed panel
The base edge has washed awayA leak, or rain running off the roofFix the leak first, then rebuild the edge

How to find a leak in a water tank

  1. Stop all water in and out. Close the inlet and every outlet valve.
  2. Mark the level. Note the water level, and check it again after 24 hours. In a roofed tank, evaporation is small, so a clear drop means a leak.
  3. Walk round the base. Look for wet ground, soft spots or washed-out sand. The wettest spot is usually closest to the leak.
  4. Check the outlet and valves. Dry them with a cloth and watch for fresh drips.
  5. Let the level fall. If the leak is in the wall area of the liner, the water stops dropping once it reaches the hole. That tells you the height to search.
  6. Look inside. Drain the tank and inspect the floor seams, the corners and the area round the outlet. Never go into a tank alone, and make sure there is fresh air.

Common causes of leaks in steel tanks

  • Liner damage. Sharp stones under the floor, tools dropped inside, roots or animals can puncture the liner.
  • Aged liner. An old liner becomes stiff and brittle, and the seams, especially at the floor, start to fail.
  • Outlet fittings. Seals perish and metal fittings corrode, so the joint where the pipe passes through the liner starts to weep.
  • Base problems. If the base settles or washes away at the edge, the liner is stretched at the foot of the wall.
  • Steel corrosion. Rust at the waterline or at the base weakens the wall. Water touching the steel means the liner is already leaking.

Repair options for each problem

ProblemRepairReplace instead when
Small hole or tear in the linerA PVC patch, glued or heat-welded onto clean, dry linerThere are many holes, or the liner cracks when folded
Split floor seamA welded repair by someone with the right equipmentSeams are failing in several places
Leaking outletNew seals or a new outlet fittingThe fitting is badly corroded
Rusted panelClean and treat surface rust; replace a panel with holesSeveral panels are holed
Washed-out baseRebuild and compact the edge; add a stone bandThe whole base has settled

In a lined tank, repair the liner, not the steel. Putty or paint on the outside of the wall will not stop a leaking liner.

When a new liner makes more sense

Fit a new liner when the old one is brittle, faded and cracking, when it has many patches, or when the seams are failing. A new liner gives the tank a fresh start for far less than a new tank, as long as the steel and base are still sound.

We sell replacement PVC tank liners in black or blue, made to order for your tank size. For a bigger job, our dam and reservoir repair team can find the leak and repair or reline the tank for you.

To stop leaks starting, follow our steel water tank maintenance checklist. If the base is the problem, see which base a steel tank needs.

Frequently asked questions

Why is my steel water tank leaking at the bottom?

Usually a hole in the floor of the liner, a split seam where the floor meets the wall, or a leaking outlet. Stones or a settled base under the floor are common causes.

Can you patch a PVC tank liner?

Yes. Small holes and tears can be patched with PVC on clean, dry liner. If the liner is old and brittle, a patch will not last and a new liner is the better choice.

How do I find a leak in a water tank?

Close all valves, mark the level and check it after 24 hours. Then look for wet ground at the base, check the outlet, and let the level fall to find the height of the leak.

Should I replace the liner or the whole tank?

If the steel panels and the base are sound, a new liner is usually enough. Replace panels only where the steel has rusted through.

Get your leaking tank fixed

Send us photos of the tank, the base and any wet spots, with the tank size. We will tell you whether it needs a repair or a new liner, and quote for it. Request a repair quote.

title: Why Is My Farm Dam Losing Water? Seepage, Evaporation and Leaks
excerpt: A farm dam loses water in three main ways: evaporation, seepage and leaks. Here is how to tell which one you have and how to stop it.
content:
Why is my farm dam losing water? Almost always for one of three reasons: evaporation into the air, seepage into the ground, or leaks at pipes, valves and tears in the liner. Each one has a different fix, so first work out which one you have.

Quick answer: the three ways a farm dam loses water

LossHow to spot itMain fix
EvaporationDam and bucket drop by the same amount in a bucket test; worst in hot, windy weatherSmaller surface, deeper water, covered storage
SeepageDam drops more than the bucket; unlined dam on sandy or gravel soil; wet ground below the wallLine the dam with HDPE or PVC
LeaksWet patches at pipes and valves; tears in the liner; troughs that overflowRepair the pipe, valve or liner

How do I tell which loss I have?

Use the bucket test. Stand a bucket of dam water in the dam for two or three days without pumping. Compare how far each one drops:

  • Same drop: the loss is evaporation.
  • Dam drops more: you also have seepage or a leak.

Our guide to finding a leak in a farm dam gives the step-by-step test and where to look.

Evaporation: losing water to sun and wind

Every open dam loses water from its surface. In much of South Africa this can be well over a metre of depth a year, most of it in hot, dry and windy months. The bigger the surface, the bigger the loss.

What helps:

  • Keep water deep, not wide. A deep dam with a small surface loses less than a shallow, spread-out one.
  • Move water into covered storage. A roofed steel water tank loses almost nothing to evaporation.
  • Shade small reservoirs. Shade nets or floating covers work on small, lined reservoirs. They are hard to justify on a large earth dam.
  • Cut the wind. A windbreak can help, but keep trees well away from the liner because roots damage it.

A liner does not stop evaporation. It stops seepage.

Seepage: losing water into the ground

An unlined earth dam loses water through its floor and walls. On sandy or gravel soil the loss can be very large. On dense clay it is usually smaller, but clay can crack when the dam dries out.

Seepage is hard to see, because the water disappears underground. Signs are a dam that drops more than the bucket, wet ground below the wall, or a dam that never fills properly. Seepage also carries on day and night, whether you use the water or not.

The lasting fix is a liner:

OptionGood forKeep in mind
HDPE linerLarge farm dams and open reservoirs in full sunWelded seams; the basin must be shaped and smooth
PVC linerSmaller dams, ponds and tanksFlexible and easy to fit; protect it from sharp stones
Clay or bentoniteSome unlined dams on suitable soilLess reliable where the soil is sandy or moves

Read about dam lining on sandy and clay soils, or see our farm dam liners.

Leaks: losing water at pipes, valves and tears

Leaks are often the cheapest losses to fix, so check them first.

  • Walk the outlet pipe and look for wet ground or green strips of grass.
  • Check every valve, trough and float valve. A stuck float can run all night.
  • On a lined dam, look for tears and holes at the waterline and open seams.
  • Fence the dam so animals do not walk on the liner.

Which fix saves the most water?

Start with what is cheap and fast, then deal with the big losses:

  1. Fix pipe, valve and trough leaks now.
  2. Patch liner tears before they grow.
  3. If the bucket test shows seepage, plan to line the dam. On sandy soil this usually saves the most water.
  4. Keep water deep and move what you can into covered tanks to cut evaporation.

Facing a dry season? See how to manage dam water levels in a drought.

Frequently asked questions

How much water does a farm dam lose to evaporation?

It depends on the climate, the season and the size of the surface. In many parts of South Africa an open dam can lose well over a metre of depth a year. The bucket test shows your own rate.

Does a dam liner stop evaporation?

No. A liner stops water soaking into the ground. To cut evaporation, reduce the surface area or move water into covered storage.

Is it worth lining an old earth dam?

If the bucket test shows seepage, often yes, especially on sandy soil. A liner keeps water you have already paid to pump or catch.

Should I pump borehole water into my dam?

Not into an unlined dam on sandy soil, because much of it will seep away. Store pumped water in a lined dam or a covered tank. See combining borehole water with a farm dam.

Why does my dam never fill up?

Either the catchment does not deliver enough runoff, or the dam loses water as fast as it comes in. Seepage through a sandy floor is a common cause.

Stop your dam losing water

title: Borehole Running Low? Signs, Causes and How Storage Helps
excerpt: How to tell if your borehole is running low, why it happens, and how a storage tank lets a weak borehole keep your farm supplied.
content:
What should you do when your borehole runs low? First confirm it is the borehole and not the pump. Then pump less, more often, into a storage tank, cut waste, and have a borehole contractor check the water level. Storage lets a weak borehole keep up by pumping gently around the clock.

Boreholes run low for many reasons, most often in long dry spells. This guide covers the warning signs, what you can do straight away, and how storage helps.

Quick answer: what to do when a borehole runs low

StepWhy
Check the pump, pipes and powerA worn pump or a leak looks like a weak borehole
Measure the water levelShows if the borehole really is dropping
Pump at a lower rate for longerGives the water time to flow back in
Store water in a covered tankBuilds a reserve from a small, steady flow
Cut leaks and wasteEvery litre saved is a litre you do not need to pump
Call a borehole contractorFor a yield test, cleaning or a deeper pump setting

Signs your borehole is running low

  • Less water at the tap or tank inlet than before, with the same pump.
  • The pump runs longer to fill the same tank.
  • Air or spluttering in the outlet, which can mean the water is near the pump intake.
  • Muddy or sandy water, or a change in taste.
  • The pump trips on its dry-run protection.

Any one of these can also come from a worn pump, a cracked pipe or low voltage. Rule those out before you blame the borehole.

Static level, pumping level and drawdown

When the pump is off, water in the borehole settles at the static water level. When the pump runs, the level drops to the pumping water level. The difference is the drawdown.

If the static level is lower than it used to be, the groundwater around you has dropped. If the drawdown is getting bigger at the same pumping rate, the borehole is struggling to keep up. A borehole contractor can measure both with a dip meter.

Why boreholes run low

  • Dry seasons and droughts mean less rain soaks in to refill the groundwater.
  • Pumping too hard pulls the level down faster than water can flow back in.
  • Clogging of the borehole screen with silt, scale or iron reduces the flow.
  • Neighbouring boreholes drawing from the same water.

How storage helps a weak borehole

A weak borehole can still supply a farm if it pumps slowly for many hours into storage. Instead of a big flow for two hours, the borehole gives a small flow for most of the day. The tank collects it and supplies the big flows when you need them.

A covered steel water tank is the best fit. It keeps the water clean and loses very little to evaporation. Size it for at least two to three days of essential use, such as livestock and the house. Our guide on borehole storage tank sizes shows how.

Ways to use less borehole water

ActionWhere the saving comes from
Fix leaking pipes, floats and troughsWater lost all day, every day
Irrigate early morning or eveningLess lost to sun and wind
Cover tanks and troughs where you canLess evaporation and less contamination
Put stock water firstAnimals cannot go without water
Collect roof rainwaterTakes load off the borehole when it rains

Plan for the next dry season

The best time to prepare is while the borehole is still strong. Ask for a yield test so you know the safe pumping rate. Record the static water level every month, at the same time of day, so you can see a drop coming. Install storage and fix leaks before the dry months, not during them.

If your area often runs short, plan for two separate supplies, such as a borehole and roof rainwater, or two boreholes. A lined farm dam that catches run-off can also carry irrigation through the summer while the borehole looks after stock.

When to call a borehole contractor

Call a registered borehole contractor if the level keeps dropping, the water turns muddy, or the pump keeps tripping. They can do a yield test, clean or re-develop the borehole, or lower the pump if it is safe to do so. Do not lower the pump yourself without knowing the borehole depth.

Frequently asked questions

How do I know if my borehole is drying up?

Watch for less flow, longer pump run times, air in the outlet and muddy water. A falling static water level, measured over weeks, confirms it.

Can a borehole recover after running low?

Often yes, when you pump less and after good rains refill the groundwater. A clogged borehole may need cleaning to recover.

How much water storage do I need if my borehole is weak?

Enough for two to three days of your essential use, filled by slow, steady pumping. If the borehole gives less per day than you use, also cut use or add another source.

Build a reserve before the next dry spell

title: Steel Water Tank and Reservoir Maintenance: A Simple Checklist
excerpt: What to check on a corrugated steel water tank or reservoir, and how often: base, bolts, rust, liner, roof, overflow and outlets.
content:
How do you maintain a steel water tank? Walk round it once a month, check the bolts, roof and rust spots every six months, and look inside at the liner and silt once a year. Most problems start small: a blocked overflow, a washed-out base edge or a weeping outlet. Catch them early and the tank lasts far longer.

This checklist works for any lined corrugated steel tank or reservoir, from a 10 000 litre farm tank to a large irrigation reservoir.

Quick answer: reservoir maintenance checklist

CheckHow oftenWhat to look for
Water level and wet groundMonthlyA level that drops with no use; wet or soft ground at the base
Outlet, valves and floatMonthlyDrips, stiff valves, a float valve that sticks
Base edge and drainageMonthly, and after heavy rainWashed-out sand, water pooling against the wall
Bolts and seamsEvery 6 monthsLoose, missing or rusted bolts; gaps at the seams
Rust on the outsideEvery 6 monthsRust spots, especially low down and at the waterline
Roof, hatch and overflowEvery 6 months, and after stormsLoose sheets, an open hatch, a blocked or unscreened overflow
Liner and silt insideYearlyHoles, brittle patches, failed seams, a layer of silt
Hold-down anchorsYearly, and after strong windLoose or corroded anchors on roofed tanks

Outside the tank

Rust starts where the steel stays damp. Keep the bottom of the wall clear of soil, grass, mulch and anything stored against it. Keep manure and fertiliser away from the steel, because they speed up corrosion.

Treat small rust spots early. Clean them back to bright metal with a wire brush, then touch them up with a zinc-rich paint. Tighten loose bolts and replace any that have rusted.

Base and drainage

The base carries the full weight of the water. If its edge washes away, the wall and liner lose support. After heavy rain, check that water runs away from the tank and does not pool against it. Rebuild a washed-out edge and add a band of stone to protect it.

Planning a new tank? Our guide to choosing a sand pad, ring beam or slab explains which base suits which tank.

Inside the tank: liner and silt

Once a year, or when the water turns cloudy, drain the tank and look inside. Check the liner for holes, brittle areas and seams that are lifting, especially at the floor and round the outlet. Scoop out silt gently with plastic tools, never with spades or sharp tools that can cut the liner.

A screen on the inlet keeps much of the silt and debris out. Never go into a tank alone, and make sure there is fresh air before anyone climbs in.

Valves, floats and pipes

Open and close every valve once a month so it does not seize. Check the float valve: if water runs from the overflow while the tank is full, the float is sticking and you are wasting water. Look along exposed pipes for drips and damage from sun, animals or vehicles.

Keep a simple logbook next to the tank. Write down the date, what you checked and anything you fixed. It shows you when problems keep coming back, and it helps whoever looks after the tank next.

Roof, hatch and overflow

Walk the roof edge from a ladder rather than standing on the roof sheets, which are not made to carry a person. Keep the hatch closed so birds, rodents and leaves stay out. Fit a screen over the overflow, and check that it is not blocked. On a roofed tank, check the hold-down anchors after strong wind, because an empty tank is light enough to lift.

Common problems and what to do

ProblemWhat to do
The level drops with no useFollow our guide to finding a leak in a steel tank
Green or cloudy waterClose the hatch, screen the inlet, and clean out silt
Rust streaks down the wallTreat the rust, and check the liner behind it for a leak
Liner brittle and crackingPlan for a replacement PVC liner

Frequently asked questions

How often should a water reservoir be cleaned?

Look inside at least once a year. Clean out silt when it builds up or when the water turns cloudy. A screened inlet means you clean less often.

How do you stop a steel water tank from rusting?

Keep the wall dry at the bottom, keep soil and fertiliser away from it, and treat small rust spots early with a zinc-rich paint. Inside, a sound liner keeps water off the steel.

Should I paint the inside of a lined steel tank?

No. The liner holds the water and protects the steel. Do not paint or glue anything onto the liner unless it is a proper liner repair.

Who can maintain a steel reservoir for me?

Damtech inspects, repairs and relines corrugated steel reservoirs. Send us photos and we will tell you what needs attention.

Need a new or bigger tank?

If your tank is past repair, or you need more storage, compare our corrugated steel water tank sizes and prices, then request a quote for supply and installation.

title: How Big Should a Borehole Storage Tank Be? A Simple Sizing Guide
excerpt: Size a borehole storage tank in three simple steps, with a worked example in litres and the standard steel water tank sizes.
content:
How big should a storage tank for a borehole be? Size the tank to how much water you use, not to the borehole. A good starting point is one to three days of your normal use. Then check that the borehole can refill the tank faster than you empty it.

This guide walks through the sizing in three simple steps, with a worked example in litres. You can also use our water calculators to work out daily use.

Quick answer: borehole storage tank size

Your situationStore this much
Steady use, reliable borehole and powerAbout 1 day of use
Livestock, or power cuts are common2 to 3 days of use
Irrigation in short, big dosesAt least one full irrigation cycle
Borehole gives less per day than you useStorage alone will not fix it. Reduce use or add a source.

Step 1: find your borehole's safe yield

The safe yield is how much water the borehole can give each day without the level dropping too far. It comes from a proper yield test done by a borehole contractor. The test report usually gives a pumping rate in litres per hour and how many hours a day to pump.

Multiply the two to get litres per day. For example: 1 500 litres per hour × 16 hours = 24 000 litres per day.

Do not guess the yield from how fast the pump runs on day one. A borehole can give a strong flow for a few hours and then drop off.

Step 2: work out how much you use per day

Add up every use: livestock, the house, garden, dip tanks, cleaning and irrigation. For irrigation, use the amount for your crop and area in the hottest month. Our calculators help with livestock and irrigation water needs. Your local agricultural adviser can also help.

Use the busiest time of year, not the average. That is when the tank matters most.

Step 3: choose how many days to store

Storage gives you a buffer for pump breakdowns, power cuts and very hot days. More days means more security, but a bigger tank. For most farms, one to three days of use is a sensible range.

Then compare with the borehole. If the safe yield per day is more than your daily use, the tank refills every day. If it is less, the tank will slowly run dry no matter how big it is.

Worked example: sizing a borehole tank

StepExample figure
Safe yield from the test1 500 litres per hour for 16 hours = 24 000 litres per day
Daily use in the hottest month20 000 litres
Days of storage wanted2 days
Storage needed20 000 × 2 = 40 000 litres
Check: does the borehole keep up?Yes. 24 000 litres in is more than 20 000 litres out each day.
Tank to chooseThe next standard size up, for example a 50 000 litre tank

These are example figures only. Use the numbers from your own yield test and your own use.

Water tank sizes for borehole storage

Our standard corrugated steel water tank kits come in these sizes. Larger tanks, up to about 500 000 litres, are made to order in diameters from 3 m to 17 m.

CapacityDiameter × height
10 000 litres3 m × 1.5 m
20 000 litres4 m × 1.5 m
50 000 litres5 m × 2.3 m
100 000 litres9 m × 1.5 m

Each product page shows the current kit price. Every tank also needs a level, firm base. Our guide to water tank base sizes explains what to build.

Where should the tank go?

Put the tank as high as you sensibly can, on firm, level ground close to where the water is used. Height gives free pressure, so water can reach troughs and the house by gravity. A short pipe run means less friction and fewer leaks.

Leave room around the tank for the base, the overflow and access for maintenance. Keep it away from big trees, whose roots and falling branches cause trouble. If the ground is soft, clay that swells, or sloping, ask us about the base before you order.

Common sizing mistakes

  • Sizing to the pump, not the use. The tank is there to cover your peak use.
  • Using winter figures. Size for the hottest, driest month.
  • Expecting storage to fix a weak borehole. If yield is below use, the tank only delays the shortage.
  • Forgetting the base and the outlet height. Water below the outlet cannot be used.

Frequently asked questions

What size is a 10 000 litre water tank?

Our 10 000 litre corrugated steel tank is 3 m in diameter and 1.5 m high.

How do I choose a water tank size?

Work out your daily use in the busiest month, multiply by the days of reserve you want (usually one to three) and pick the next standard size up.

What size tank do I need for borehole irrigation?

At least enough to run one full irrigation cycle, so the system is not limited by the borehole's flow while it runs. Then check the borehole can refill it before the next cycle.

Can a bigger tank make up for a weak borehole?

Only for a while. If the borehole gives less water per day than you use, any tank will eventually run dry.

Get the right tank size

Send us your yield test figures and what the water is for. We will recommend a tank size and quote it. Request a steel water tank quote.

title: Corrugated Steel Reservoirs vs Earth Dams and Plastic Tanks: Costs and Benefits
excerpt: What a corrugated steel reservoir costs to own, where it saves water, and when an earth dam or plastic tanks make more sense on a South African farm.
content:
Is a corrugated steel reservoir worth the money on a farm? In most cases, yes, when you need between about 10 000 and 500 000 litres close to where the water is used. A lined, roofed steel reservoir loses very little water and goes up quickly. An earth dam is cheaper for very large volumes, but it loses water to seepage and evaporation. Plastic tanks suit small volumes.

This guide compares the three options in plain terms, so you can decide what fits your farm before you ask for prices.

Quick answer: steel reservoir, earth dam or plastic tanks?

OptionBest forMain drawback
Corrugated steel reservoirAbout 10 000 to 500 000+ litres, next to a borehole, camp or fieldNeeds a level, well-drained base, and the liner wears over time
Unlined earth damVery large volumes on clay that holds water, where there is spaceSeepage and evaporation, and silt fills it over time
Lined earth damLarge volumes on sandy or leaky groundThe open surface still evaporates
Plastic tanksSmall volumes, for a house or a single troughLarge volumes need many tanks joined together

What is a corrugated steel reservoir?

A corrugated steel reservoir is a round tank built from curved, corrugated steel panels. The panels are bolted together on site, ring by ring. A PVC liner inside holds the water, and a roof is optional. In Afrikaans it is often called a sinkdam.

Damtech builds them in Z275 galvanised steel or AZ150 Aluzinc. Both come with a 550 gsm PVC liner and a geotextile floor sheet as standard. Because the tank is bolted, it can later be extended, relined or moved.

What does a steel reservoir cost to own?

The price depends on more than the tank itself. These are the parts that make up the total:

Cost itemWhat drives it
Tank kitDiameter, height and steel type (galvanised or Aluzinc)
BaseSand pad, concrete ring beam or slab, depending on tank size and ground
LinerLiner thickness; a heavier liner is available on request
Roof and fittingsRoof or no roof, inlet, outlet, overflow and valves
Transport and installationDistance to site and how easy the site is to reach
UpkeepLow: regular checks, cleaning out silt, and in time a new liner

We publish fixed prices for our standard tank kits on the steel water storage tanks page. For larger reservoirs, the base and installation are quoted for your site. Our guide to choosing a sand pad, ring beam or slab explains the base options.

Where do you lose water: steel reservoir or earth dam?

Every open water surface loses water to the sun and wind. The bigger the surface, the more you lose. An unlined dam also loses water downward into the soil, and sandy soil loses the most.

A roofed steel reservoir keeps the sun off the water, so evaporation is small. The liner stops seepage. That makes a steel reservoir a good way to hold borehole water you have paid to pump. If you already have a dam that leaks, read about lining a dam on sandy or clay soil.

Benefits of a steel reservoir on a farm

  • Little water lost. The liner stops seepage, and a roof cuts evaporation.
  • Quick to build. The panels go up on a prepared base, without the large earthworks a dam needs.
  • Placed where you need it. Put it next to the borehole, the camps or the field, so pipes and pumping stay short.
  • Cleaner water. No mud floor, no trampled banks, and a roof keeps out leaves, birds and sunlight.
  • Flexible. You can add rings, reline it or move it later.

Drawbacks to plan for

  • The liner is the part that wears. Check it, keep sharp objects out, and budget for a new liner one day.
  • The zinc coating is thin. Soft or acidic water attacks it faster. Our guide to galvanised steel water tanks explains why the liner matters so much.
  • It needs a proper base. The base must be level, firm and well drained.
  • Roofed tanks need anchors. An empty tank with a roof is light enough for strong wind to lift.
  • There is a size limit. For millions of litres, a dam is usually the cheaper way to store water.

Which storage option suits your farm?

Your situationA good choice
Drinking water in several campsSteel tanks with troughs at each water point
A buffer between a borehole and irrigationA steel reservoir next to the borehole or field
Very large seasonal storage with a good dam siteAn earth dam, lined if the soil leaks
A house or one troughA small steel or plastic tank

Frequently asked questions

What is a sink dam?

"Sinkdam" is the Afrikaans name for a corrugated steel dam or reservoir. It is a round tank of bolted, corrugated steel panels with a liner inside to hold the water.

Are corrugated steel dams better than earth dams?

For small and medium volumes, usually yes, because they lose far less water and take up less space. For very large volumes on a good dam site, an earth dam is normally cheaper per litre.

How long does a corrugated steel reservoir last?

It depends mostly on the liner, the water chemistry and how well the base drains. Good maintenance makes a big difference. We would rather assess your water and site than quote a number of years.

Does a steel reservoir need a roof?

Not always, but a roof cuts evaporation, keeps the water cleaner and slows algae. Drinking water for people should always be covered.

What size steel reservoir do I need?

Work from your daily use and how many days of storage you want. Our water storage calculators help you put numbers on it.

title: Managing Farm Dam Water Levels in a Drought: Make the Water Last
excerpt: A simple plan for a farm dam in a drought: measure the water, set trigger levels, put water to its most important use and cut avoidable losses.
content:
How do you manage a farm dam in a drought? Measure the water level every week, work out how many days of water you have left, and decide in advance what you will cut back at each level. Then protect the water you have from avoidable losses and poor quality.

This guide is about running a dam through a dry spell. If you are getting ready for the coming El Niño summer, also read how to drought-proof your farm dam.

Quick answer: a drought plan for your dam

StepWhat to doWhy
1. MeasureRead a gauge board on the same day every weekYou see the trend early
2. Count the daysWater left ÷ water used per dayYou know how long it will last
3. Set trigger levelsDecide now what you cut at each levelNo panic decisions later
4. Put water first where it mattersPeople, then animals, then cropsProtects what cannot wait
5. Cut lossesFix leaks, keep water deep, store in covered tanksMore water for use

How much water is left in my dam?

Put a gauge board in the dam: a post marked every 100 mm, fixed where you can read it from the bank. Read it at the same time each week and write the number down.

Then turn the level into a volume. Our guide on how to calculate dam capacity shows how. Work out the volume at a few levels once, and keep the list with the gauge readings.

Now count the days:

Days of water left = water left ÷ water used per day

For example, 900 m³ left and 15 m³ used a day gives about 60 days. Evaporation and leaks take their share too, so the real number will be lower.

Set trigger levels before you need them

A trigger level is a mark on the gauge board where you change how you use the water. Set them while the dam is still full.

LevelExample action
FullNormal use; check the dam and pipes for leaks
Trigger 1Stop or cut back irrigation; water only the most valuable crops
Trigger 2Livestock and household only; sell or move animals if the rains are far off
ReserveEmergency use only; bring in water from a borehole, tank or carting

Set the triggers by days of water left, not by depth alone. Most dams have sloping sides, so the top metre holds far more water than the bottom metre. A dam that looks half full by depth can hold much less than half its water.

Who gets the water first?

Write down the order before the pressure is on. A common order is:

  1. Drinking water and household use.
  2. Livestock and game drinking water.
  3. Permanent crops and orchards that would die without water.
  4. Annual crops and everything else.

Cut the losses you can control

  • Keep water deep. A shallow, wide dam loses more to evaporation than a deep, narrow one. If you have several dams, use the shallow ones first and keep the deep one.
  • Use covered storage. Water in a covered steel tank loses almost nothing to evaporation. See our steel water tanks.
  • Find and fix leaks. Do the bucket test in our guide to finding a leak in a farm dam.
  • Irrigate early or late. Watering in the cool of the day loses less to the air.
  • Check troughs and float valves. A stuck float valve can run all night.

Watch the water quality as the level drops

As the water drops, salts and dirt become more concentrated. Algae grow more easily in warm, shallow water. Animals that walk into a low dam stir up mud and foul the water.

  • Give animals a trough instead of walking into the dam.
  • Look for green scum or a bad smell, and test the water if you are worried.
  • Read our guide to farm dam water quality for livestock.

Use the low water to fix the dam

A nearly empty dam is the best time to work on it. You can remove silt, check the liner, repair the wall and line an unlined dam before the rains come. Every litre saved from seepage is a litre for the next dry spell. Compare HDPE and PVC dam liner options.

For the bigger picture this season, see what El Niño 2026/27 means for farm water.

Frequently asked questions

How long will my dam water last?

Divide the water left by the water you use per day. Then allow for evaporation and any leaks, which shorten the time. Recheck it every week.

How often should I check my dam level in a drought?

Once a week, on the same day and time. Check more often when you are close to a trigger level.

Why does the level drop faster when the dam is low?

A dam with sloping sides gets narrower as it gets deeper. The same amount of water used each day takes the level down further when the surface is smaller.

Should I line my dam during a drought?

It is often the best time. The basin is dry or nearly dry, so it can be shaped and lined before the next rain fills it.

If your dam needs repairs or a liner, tell us its size and condition. We will help you get it done while the water is low.

title: Protecting Farm Water During Power Cuts and Load-Shedding
excerpt: When the power goes, pumps stop and water can turn bad. Simple ways to keep farm water clean and flowing during power cuts and load-shedding.
content:
How do you protect farm water during power cuts and load-shedding? Store enough water to last through the outage, keep it in a covered tank, feed troughs by gravity, and fit a non-return valve, float valve and overflow. Then the water stays clean and keeps flowing when the pumps stop.

When the power goes, pumps, aerators and treatment equipment stop. Water stops moving, troughs run dry and dirty water can flow back into clean supplies. This guide shows simple ways to prevent that.

Quick answer: protecting stored water during power cuts

Problem when the power is offSimple fix
Pumps stop and troughs run dryStore a reserve and feed troughs by gravity
Water flows back down the pipeFit a non-return valve on the pump line
Tanks overflow when power returnsFloat valve or level switch, and an overflow pipe led away
Dust, birds and animals get into open waterCovered tank and fenced dam
Still, warm water grows algaeCover the water and keep it moving when you can

Why power cuts put farm water at risk

  • Pumps stop. Borehole and transfer pumps cannot refill tanks, so troughs and the house run dry.
  • Backflow. When a pump stops, water in the pipe can run back down. Dirty water can be pulled into a clean line.
  • No aeration or treatment. Electric aerators, filters and chlorinators stop. Still, warm water in an open dam can grow algae.
  • Surges and overflows. When power returns, pumps restart all at once. Tanks without a float valve can overflow and wash out their base.
  • Animals look for water. Thirsty stock push into dams and wet edges, which muddies the water and can damage liners.

Store enough water for the outage

Work out how long your longest outages last and how much you use in that time. Add a margin for hot days. Many farms aim for at least one to two days of essential use, so stock and the house never depend on the pump. Our borehole storage sizing guide shows how to work this out.

Let gravity do the work

A tank on higher ground, or on a raised base, can feed troughs and the house with no power at all. Even a few metres of height gives useful pressure for troughs. This is the simplest way to keep water flowing during load-shedding.

Fit the right valves

FittingWhat it does
Non-return valveStops water running back down the pipe when the pump stops
Float valve or level switchStops filling when the tank is full, so it cannot overflow
Overflow pipeLeads any extra water away from the tank base
Dry-run protection on the pumpStops the pump if the borehole level drops too low

Keep stored water clean

  • Cover drinking water. A steel tank with a roof keeps out dust, leaves, birds and animals.
  • Fence open dams and give stock a trough instead of open access to the water's edge.
  • Keep the inlet and outlet apart so water moves through the tank instead of sitting in one corner.
  • Clean troughs regularly, especially after outages when water sat still.
  • Check the liner after animals have been in or around a dam. See our guide on farm dam water quality for livestock.

A simple checklist before outages

  1. Fill every tank to the top before a scheduled outage.
  2. Check float valves close properly and overflow pipes are clear.
  3. Test the non-return valve: the pipe should stay full after the pump stops.
  4. Make sure troughs fed by gravity are working and clean.
  5. Close valves to areas that can wait, so stock and the house get water first.
  6. After the outage, check that pumps restarted and tanks are filling.

Put the checklist on the pump house door so anyone on the farm can follow it.

Backup power for pumps

A solar pump, or a generator for the main pump, can keep water moving through long outages. Even so, storage is still the cheapest buffer. A full tank keeps working even when the backup power fails.

If you add a solar pump, size the tank to carry you through the night and cloudy days. The pump fills the tank while the sun shines, and the tank supplies water the rest of the time. A generator works best on a timer or with a level switch, so it only runs when the tank actually needs water.

Frequently asked questions

How do I keep water for my livestock during load-shedding?

Keep at least a day or two of their water in a covered tank above the troughs. Gravity then feeds the troughs while the pump is off.

Why does my tank overflow after a power cut?

When power returns, the pump restarts and keeps filling. Fit a float valve or level switch to stop it when the tank is full, and an overflow pipe led away from the base.

Can dirty water get into my supply when the pump stops?

Yes, through backflow. A non-return valve on the pump line stops water running back down the pipe.

Plan storage that keeps working

title: Borehole Water Storage: Steel Tank or Lined Farm Dam?
excerpt: Steel tank or lined farm dam for borehole water? When each one works, how to combine them, and what to test before you irrigate with borehole water.
content:
Should you store borehole water in a tank or a lined farm dam? For most farms the answer is a lined steel tank for daily water, and a lined dam only when you need very large volumes. A borehole gives a small, steady flow. Storage lets that flow build up so you have enough water when you need a lot at once.

This guide explains how a borehole and storage work together, when a tank is the better choice, when a dam makes sense, and what to check before you use borehole water for irrigation.

Quick answer: borehole water storage options

OptionBest forWatch out for
Lined steel tankDaily water for stock, the house and small irrigation blocksSize it to your daily use, not to the borehole
Lined farm damLarge volumes for irrigation, filled by borehole and run-offEvaporation from the open surface, and a liner that must suit the soil
Tank and dam togetherFarms that irrigate and also need clean water for stockKeep the clean tank water separate from dam water
No storage (pump straight to use)Very small, steady uses onlyThe pump starts and stops often and you have no reserve

Why does a borehole need storage?

A borehole can only give water as fast as the ground lets it flow back in. That rate is its yield, usually measured in litres per hour. Most farm boreholes give a modest yield that does not change much from day to day.

Your use is different. Cattle drink most in the heat of the day. Irrigation needs a big flow for a few hours. The house uses most in the morning and evening. Storage sits between the two. The borehole fills it slowly, and you draw from it quickly when you need to.

Storage also helps the borehole itself. A pump that runs long, steady cycles into a tank works more gently than one that starts and stops every few minutes. You can also pump when power is available, or when electricity is cheaper, and use the water later.

When is a steel tank the better choice?

A lined corrugated steel tank suits most borehole systems. Choose a tank when:

  • You need clean water. A tank with a roof keeps out dust, leaves, birds and animals. The water stays close to the quality it had in the borehole.
  • You want to lose less water. A covered tank loses very little to evaporation. An open dam loses water every sunny, windy day.
  • You need water higher up. A tank on a good base can feed troughs and the house by gravity, so water still flows when the power is off.
  • Space is limited. A tank holds a lot of water on a small, level footprint.

Our corrugated steel water tanks come in standard kits from 10 000 to 100 000 litres, and much larger tanks are made to order.

When does a lined farm dam make sense?

A dam makes sense when you need far more water than a tank can hold, mostly for irrigation. A dam can also collect rain run-off, so the borehole only tops it up. For large volumes, a lined earth dam is usually cheaper per litre stored than steel tanks.

The trade-offs are evaporation, algae in warm water, and the need for a liner that suits your soil. If you go this way, read our guide on dam lining for sandy and clay soils and see our farm dam liners.

Can you use a tank and a dam together?

Yes, and many farms do. A simple set-up looks like this:

  1. The borehole fills a covered steel tank first. This is the clean supply for the house and stock.
  2. When the tank is full, a float valve stops the inflow, or the extra water goes to the dam.
  3. The dam holds the bulk irrigation water, topped up by rain and the borehole.

Keep the two supplies apart. Do not pump dam water back into the drinking-water tank.

Is borehole water good for irrigation?

Often yes, but not always. Borehole water picks up minerals from the rock it sits in. Some boreholes give soft, clean water. Others give water that is salty, hard, or high in iron. Have your water tested by an accredited laboratory before you plan irrigation.

What the test showsWhat it can do
High salt (high electrical conductivity)Builds up in the soil and stresses sensitive crops
High iron or manganeseStains and can clog drippers and filters
Hard water (lots of calcium)Leaves scale on fittings and emitters
BacteriaNot fit for drinking without treatment

Water stored in an open dam slowly gets saltier as it evaporates. That is one more reason to keep high-quality water in a covered tank.

Borehole irrigation systems: what to plan

  • Know the safe yield. Ask your borehole contractor for a proper yield test. Pump at or below the recommended rate.
  • Size the storage to your use. See our guide on how big a borehole storage tank should be.
  • Use the height you have. A tank on higher ground can feed drip lines by gravity or with a smaller booster pump.
  • Filter before drippers. Especially if the water has iron or sand in it.
  • Protect the pump. A level switch or float that stops the pump when the tank is full, or when the borehole level drops, saves pumps.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best storage tank for borehole water?

A covered, lined steel tank sized for one to three days of your use. It keeps the water clean, loses very little to evaporation and lets the borehole run steady cycles.

Can I pump borehole water straight into a dam?

Yes, for irrigation water. Expect some loss to evaporation and seepage if the dam is not lined. Keep drinking water for people and stock in a covered tank.

Is borehole water good for irrigation?

It depends on the water. Test it for salt, iron, hardness and bacteria first. Many boreholes are fine for irrigation, but salty or iron-rich water needs a plan.

Do I still need storage if my borehole is strong?

Usually yes. Even a strong borehole cannot match the short, high flows that irrigation and stock need. Storage also gives you water when the pump or the power fails.
