title: Farm Dam Water Quality for Livestock: Simple Checks and Fixes
excerpt: The warning signs of poor farm dam water, how to test it, and practical ways to keep livestock drinking water clean, from fencing to troughs.
content:
Is your farm dam water safe for livestock? Watch for blue-green scum, a bad smell, very muddy water, dead fish or animals that drink less than usual. Any of these is a warning sign. Move the animals to another water source, have the water tested by a laboratory, and speak to your vet.

This guide explains what the signs mean, how to test the water and how to keep dam water cleaner for your stock.

Quick answer: what the warning signs mean

What you seePossible causeFirst step
Blue-green scum or a paint-like filmBlue-green algae (cyanobacteria), which can be toxicKeep animals away, test the water, call your vet
Muddy brown waterSoil washed in, or animals trampling the banksFence the dam and water from a trough
Bad smell or dead fishLow oxygen and rotting materialStop using the water and have it tested
Thick green weed or algaeToo many nutrients from manure or fertiliserCut run-off into the dam
Animals drink less or fall illMany possible causes, water among themCall your vet and test the water

Why farm dam water goes bad

Three things work together. Rain washes manure, fertiliser and soil into the dam. Warm, shallow, still water lets algae grow fast. And animals that walk into the dam stir up mud and leave dung in the water.

Drought makes it worse. As the level drops, the water gets warmer and shallower, and whatever is in it becomes more concentrated. Our guide to managing farm dam water levels in a drought covers this in more detail.

How to check farm dam water quality

  • Look every week in hot weather. Check the colour, any scum on the surface, the smell and the edges of the dam.
  • Watch your animals. Drinking less, or avoiding the water, is often the first sign.
  • Use a simple test kit. Kits for pH, nitrate and cloudiness are useful for spotting changes over time.
  • Send a sample to a laboratory. Do this when something looks wrong, and before you rely on a new source. The laboratory compares the results with the South African water quality guidelines for livestock watering.

Take samples the same way each time: from the same spot, at the same depth, in a clean bottle the laboratory supplies. Note the date, the water level and the weather, so you can compare results over time.

Do not guess about blue-green algae. Some types produce toxins that can kill livestock, and you cannot tell which by looking.

How to improve water quality on a farm

FixWhat it does
Fence the dam and supply troughsStops trampling and dung in the water
Keep a grass strip round the damSlows run-off and catches soil and nutrients
Move kraals and feeding areas away from inflowsKeeps manure out of the water
Build a small silt trap upstreamCatches mud before it reaches the dam
Line the damNo mud floor or banks to stir up, and less water lost to seepage
Store drinking water in a covered tankDark, cool water grows far less algae

Start with the cheapest fixes. A fence and a trough often make the biggest difference, because they stop the daily trampling and dung that keep the water dirty. Lining the dam makes most sense when it also leaks, so you fix water loss and water quality together. Our guide to lining a dam on sandy or clay soil explains the options.

Water storage for livestock: pump to a tank and trough

The simplest way to protect livestock water is to keep animals out of the dam. Pump from the dam or borehole into a covered tank, and feed troughs from the tank. A roof keeps out sunlight, so algae struggle to grow, and the water stays cooler.

A steel livestock water trough fed from a corrugated steel tank gives every camp its own clean water point. For drought planning, see our guide to livestock water, tanks and troughs in a drought.

Frequently asked questions

How do I improve water quality in my farm dam?

Keep manure, fertiliser and soil out of it, and keep animals out of the water. Fence the dam, keep a grass strip round it and water the stock from troughs.

Is blue-green algae dangerous to cattle?

It can be. Some blue-green algae produce toxins that can make livestock very ill or kill them. Keep animals away from any dam with a blue-green scum and get the water tested.

How often should I test my dam water?

Look at it weekly in summer. Send a sample to a laboratory when anything changes, and before relying on a new water source.

What is the best water storage for livestock?

A covered tank feeding troughs. The water stays cooler, cleaner and darker than in an open dam, and animals cannot walk into it.

title: Lined Farm Dams: Dam Lining on Sandy, Clay and Rocky Soil
excerpt: How sandy, clay, rocky and soft soils affect a farm dam, why many South African dams need a liner, and which lining suits each kind of ground.
content:
Does a farm dam on sandy or clay soil need a liner? On sandy soil, almost always: water drains straight through sand. On clay, sometimes: good clay holds water, but it cracks when it dries out and some clays wash away. A welded HDPE or PVC liner stops both problems. This guide shows how each soil behaves and which lining suits it.

Quick answer: which lining for which soil?

SoilMain problemUsual solution
SandyWater drains away through the floor and banksHDPE or PVC liner on a smooth, compacted base
ClayCracks when dry; some clays erode in waterGood clay can work; a liner is safer if the level drops often
LoamLeaks slowly, varies across the siteLiner, after a soil check
Rocky or stonySharp stones puncture a linerThicker liner on geotextile, with the base cleared
Soft or organicSettles unevenly and stretches the linerRemove soft material, build a firm base, then line

Why soil decides whether a dam holds water

An unlined dam is only as tight as the ground it is dug into. Water always looks for a way out. The size of the soil grains decides how easily it gets through.

Farm dams on sandy soil

Sand has large grains with big gaps between them. Water runs through it quickly, so an unlined dam on sand can lose a large share of its water into the ground. Sand is also hard to compact and its banks erode easily.

A geomembrane liner, such as HDPE or PVC sheet, is the usual answer. Sand itself makes a good base for a liner once it is smoothed and compacted, because it has no sharp edges. The banks must be shaped to a stable slope first.

Farm dams on clay soil

Clay has very fine grains. Well-compacted clay at the right moisture lets very little water through. That is why many older farm dams were built without a liner.

Clay has two weak points:

  • Cracking: when the water level drops in a dry spell, the exposed clay dries and cracks. When the dam fills again, water runs into the cracks.
  • Dispersive clay: some South African clays break apart in water and wash away. Water can then form tunnels through the bank. A simple soil test, such as a crumb test, shows whether a clay is dispersive.

If your dam level swings a lot, or the clay is dispersive, a liner is the safer choice.

Loam, rocky and soft ground

Loam is a mix of sand, silt and clay. It often leaks slowly, and the mix can change across one site. A liner on a prepared base gives a predictable result.

Rocky or stony ground is the main danger for a liner. Stones push through the sheet once the dam is full. The base must be cleared and raked, and a geotextile cushion laid under the liner. A thicker liner adds puncture resistance.

Soft or organic soil settles under the weight of water. Uneven settling stretches and tears a liner. The soft layer should be removed or stabilised before lining.

Lining options compared

OptionProsCons
Compacted clayLow material cost if good clay is on siteCracks when dry; needs careful compaction; needs upkeep
HDPE linerVery low leakage; strong in sun; suits large damsNeeds skilled welding and a smooth base
PVC linerFlexible; fits corners and small pondsLess suited to large dams in full sun
Liner on geotextileProtects the liner on rough groundExtra material and labour

For more on how the materials differ, read our guide to HDPE dam liners and our HDPE, PVC and bitumen comparison.

How to choose for your site

  1. Find out what your soil is. Dig a few test holes in the floor and banks. Feel the soil and look at the layers.
  2. Watch the dam. If it drops quickly after rain stops, it is probably leaking into the ground.
  3. Think about how the dam is used. A dam for irrigation or livestock that must stay full justifies a liner.
  4. Prepare the base well. Whatever the soil, the base must be firm, smooth and free of stones and roots.

Our dam lining calculator gives a first estimate of the liner area for your dam size.

Frequently asked questions

Can you build a farm dam in sandy soil?

Yes, but it needs a liner. Sand drains water too fast for an unlined dam to hold water reliably.

Do clay dams need a liner?

Not always. A dam in good, well-compacted clay can hold water. A liner is the safer choice if the clay is dispersive or the water level drops often and the banks crack.

What goes under a dam liner?

A smooth, compacted soil base, cleared of stones and roots. On rough or stony ground, a geotextile cushion goes between the soil and the liner.

Which dam liner is best for a farm dam?

For most earth farm dams in full sun, HDPE. PVC suits smaller ponds and steel tanks. The soil, size and use decide.

title: How to Calculate Farm Dam Capacity: A Simple Worked Example
excerpt: Work out how much water your farm dam holds with simple formulas for lined, round and natural earth dams, plus a worked example.
content:
How do you calculate how much water a dam holds? For a dam with straight, sloping sides, multiply the average length × average width × depth. That gives cubic metres. Multiply by 1 000 to get litres. Natural earth dams need a rougher estimate, shown below.

Quick answer: dam capacity formulas

Dam shapeFormulaHow accurate
Dug dam with sloping sides (rectangular)Average length × average width × depthGood
Round tank or dam with straight sides3.14 × radius × radius × depthGood
Natural earth dam in a valley0.4 × surface area × deepest depthRough estimate only

Average length means the length at the top plus the length at the floor, divided by two. The same goes for the width.

UnitEquals
1 cubic metre (m³)1 000 litres (1 kilolitre)
1 000 m³1 megalitre (1 million litres)

Worked example: a lined farm dam

Say your dam is 30 m long and 20 m wide at the top. The sides slope in, so the floor is 24 m by 14 m. The water is 3 m deep when full.

  1. Average length: (30 + 24) ÷ 2 = 27 m
  2. Average width: (20 + 14) ÷ 2 = 17 m
  3. Volume: 27 × 17 × 3 = about 1 380 m³
  4. In litres: 1 380 × 1 000 = about 1.38 million litres (1.38 megalitres)

This method is close enough for planning. A surveyor or engineer can give an exact figure if you need one.

Worked example: a natural earth dam

An earth dam in a valley has no neat shape. A common rule of thumb is:

Volume ≈ 0.4 × surface area × deepest depth

Pace out or measure the water surface. Say it covers about 2 000 m² and the deepest point is 3 m. The dam holds roughly 0.4 × 2 000 × 3 = 2 400 m³, or about 2.4 million litres.

Treat this as a rough guide. The real figure can be quite different if the dam is unusually steep or flat.

Worked example: a round tank or dam

For a round dam or tank with straight sides, use the radius (half the width). A tank 10 m wide and 2.3 m deep holds:

3.14 × 5 × 5 × 2.3 = about 181 m³, or about 181 000 litres.

Our steel water tank sizes list the capacity of each tank, so you do not have to work it out.

Full capacity is not usable water

  • Measure to the spillway. The dam is full when water reaches the spillway, not the top of the wall.
  • Water below the outlet stays behind. If the pipe sits above the floor, you cannot draw the bottom water by gravity.
  • Silt takes up space. Older dams fill with silt and hold less than they did when built.
  • Losses take their share. Evaporation and seepage cut what you can use. See why a farm dam loses water.

How big should my dam be?

Size the dam for the dry season, not the average year:

  1. Work out how much water you use per day for the house, animals and crops.
  2. Multiply by the number of days the dam must last without rain.
  3. Add extra for evaporation, seepage and a dry year.

When the dam fills depends on where you farm. Most of the summer rainfall areas get their rain from about October to March. The Western Cape gets most of its rain in winter, roughly May to August. Plan for the months between rains.

Only part of the rain that falls on the catchment runs into the dam. Bigger dams and new walls also need a properly sized spillway, so speak to an engineer before building one.

Our water storage and dam lining calculators help you work out how much water you need and how much liner a dam takes.

How much liner does the example dam need?

For the 30 m × 20 m example, the floor is 336 m² and the four sloping sides add about 373 m². That is about 710 m² before the extra needed for the anchor trench and seam overlaps. The calculator adds those for you. See our farm dam liners for the options.

Frequently asked questions

How do I calculate dam water capacity?

For a dug dam: average length × average width × depth, in metres. The answer is in cubic metres. Multiply by 1 000 for litres.

How many litres are in a cubic metre?

1 000 litres. A megalitre is 1 000 cubic metres, or one million litres.

How accurate is the 0.4 rule for earth dams?

It is a rough estimate for dams in a natural valley. Use it for planning, not for buying or selling water rights or designing a wall.

Is there a dam capacity calculator?

Yes. Our calculators work out water needs and liner area. For the volume of an existing dam, the formulas above are quick and good enough for planning.

Does silt reduce dam capacity?

Yes. Silt settles on the floor and takes the place of water. A dry spell is a good time to remove it.

title: Reservoir Maintenance: Weeds, Reeds and Tree Roots Around a Lined Dam
excerpt: How tree roots, reeds and weeds damage lined dams and reservoirs, how far to keep trees back, and a simple plan for keeping the edge clear.
content:
Do plants and tree roots damage a lined dam or reservoir? Yes, slowly. Roots grow towards water, get under the liner edge and lift it. Reeds root in mud on the liner, and leaves and branches foul the water. The fix is simple: keep a strip of short grass round the dam, keep trees well back, and pull out reeds and seedlings while they are small.

Quick answer: plants around a lined dam

PlantRiskWhat to do
Trees and shrubsRoots lift the liner edge; branches fall in; leaves foul the waterKeep them back at least as far as they will grow tall
Reeds and bulrushesRoot in sediment on the liner and spread fastPull out early; remove the sediment they grow in
Woody weedsGrow in the anchor trench and through tearsRemove by hand while small
Short grassLow risk; holds the bank against erosionKeep it, and keep it short

How plants damage a dam liner

Most dam liners resist a single root pressing on them. The damage comes from where plants find a way in:

  • Under the edge. Roots follow moist soil into the anchor trench and under the liner. As they thicken, they lift and stretch the sheet.
  • Through existing damage. A small tear or a weak seam gives a root or reed a gap to grow through, and the gap gets bigger.
  • On top of the liner. Mud settles on the floor and slopes. Reeds root in it and their roots and stems rub and trap the liner.
  • From above. Branches fall onto the liner and puncture it. Leaves rot in the water.

How far should trees be from a dam?

A simple rule of thumb: keep trees at least as far from the dam edge as they will grow tall. Roots often spread wider than the crown, and near water they grow towards it. Thirsty trees such as willows, poplars and gums are the worst, so give them more room or remove them.

Many trees that grow along South African farm dams are also declared invasive aliens. Before you plant anything near a dam, check that it is not on the invasive list.

Reeds, bulrushes and water weeds

Reeds and bulrushes spread quickly through mud and shallow water. In a lined dam, they need sediment to root in. Remove both:

  1. Pull young plants out by hand, roots and all.
  2. Remove the mud they grow in, using soft tools or a pump. Never dig with a spade or blade on the liner.
  3. Find where the mud comes from. Stop soil washing in from bare ground near the inlet or the banks.

If you must use a herbicide, use only one registered for use near water and follow the label exactly. Many herbicides harm fish, livestock and the water you want to use.

A simple vegetation maintenance plan

WhenTask
Every monthWalk the crest. Pull seedlings and weeds from the anchor trench and the liner edge.
In the growing seasonMow or brush-cut the grass strip. Keep the liner edge visible.
After stormsRemove fallen branches and floating debris before they rub the liner.
Once a yearRemove sediment and reeds when the water is low. Cut back trees that are getting too close.

Combine this with the liner checks in our farm dam maintenance guide.

Why short grass is good

Bare soil around a dam erodes. Rain carries the soil into the water and onto the liner, where reeds can then grow. A strip of short, shallow-rooted grass holds the soil in place and makes the liner edge easy to see. Keep it mowed so it does not hide damage or burrows.

Fence the dam if livestock graze nearby. Hooves break up the grass strip and damage the liner on the slopes.

Water quality benefits

Leaves, seeds and dead plants add nutrients to the water as they rot. Extra nutrients feed algae, which can make water smell, block filters and harm livestock. Keeping plants and debris out of a reservoir is one of the simplest ways to keep its water clean. Read more about farm dam water quality for livestock.

Frequently asked questions

How do you maintain a water reservoir?

Check the liner edge and the water level every month, keep plants and debris out, remove sediment once a year and repair damage straight away.

Can tree roots grow through a dam liner?

Roots seldom push straight through an intact liner. They get under the edge and through existing tears, and lift and stretch the sheet from there.

Should there be grass around a dam?

Yes, short grass is good. It stops erosion and keeps mud off the liner. Keep it mowed and keep trees and shrubs out of the strip.

How do I get rid of reeds in a lined dam?

Pull them out while young and remove the sediment they grow in. Then stop soil from washing into the dam.

title: HDPE vs PVC vs Bitumen Dam Liners: Which Plastic Dam Lining Fits?
excerpt: A plain comparison of HDPE, PVC and bitumen dam linings: what each material is, where it works best, and how each affects water quality and the land.
content:
Which dam lining should you choose: HDPE, PVC or bitumen? Use HDPE for earth dams in full sun, PVC for steel tanks and small ponds, and bitumen torch-on for concrete and masonry dams and some earth dams. All three stop seepage well when installed properly. They differ in how they are joined, how they handle sun and shape, and what they leave behind. This guide compares them simply.

Quick answer: dam lining materials compared

MaterialBest forHow it is joinedIn the sun
HDPEEarth dams, mining ponds, large reservoirsHeat-welded on siteMade for full exposure
PVCSteel tanks, small ponds, detailed shapesFactory-welded panels, site welds or bondingLasts best covered or in a roofed tank
Bitumen torch-onConcrete and masonry dams and reservoirsTorched and bonded to the surfaceDurable with a mineral or coated finish

HDPE dam liners

HDPE (high-density polyethylene) is a stiff, black plastic sheet. Carbon black in the plastic protects it from the sun, so it can lie exposed for many years. Sheets are joined on site with heat welds that can be tested with air.

HDPE resists most salts, acids and fertiliser residues. That is why it is also used for mining and process water. It is stiff, so it suits large, open areas better than tight corners.

More detail: our HDPE dam liner guide.

PVC dam liners

PVC (polyvinyl chloride) liners are flexible sheets, often made up into panels in a factory. Because they fold easily, they fit round steel tanks, ponds and shapes with many corners. They are lighter to handle on site.

PVC is made flexible with plasticisers. Over many years in strong sun, some of these can be lost and the sheet becomes stiffer. That is why PVC lasts longest where it is shaded or covered. Our corrugated steel water tanks use a PVC liner because it folds neatly into the round tank.

Bitumen torch-on dam lining

Torch-on is a bitumen membrane reinforced with a fabric. It is heated with a gas torch so it melts onto the surface and bonds to it. It suits rigid dams and reservoirs of concrete or masonry, where the lining must stick to the structure. It is also used on some earth dams, like our bitumen-lined earth dam in Worcester.

The surface underneath must be sound, clean and dry. Cracks in the concrete are repaired first. Bitumen is softer in summer heat and stiffer in winter, so the right grade and a protective finish matter on exposed walls. Torching uses an open flame, so it needs trained installers and care near dry grass.

Water quality and drinking water

  • All three are widely used to hold irrigation and livestock water.
  • If the water is for people to drink, ask for a product that is certified for drinking water. Not every liner is.
  • Dark liners warm the water in summer, which can help algae grow. Shade, depth and keeping fertiliser runoff out matter more than the liner colour.
  • A liner stops dissolved salts and nutrients in the soil from mixing with the stored water, and stops stored water from carrying them into the ground.

Our guide to farm dam water quality for livestock covers what to test.

Effect on the land and the environment

Every lining has an environmental cost. The question is which one is smallest for your job.

PointHDPEPVCBitumen
Made fromOil-based plasticPlastic with plasticisersOil-based bitumen and fabric
InstallationHeat weldingWelding or bondingOpen gas flame and fumes
Water savedHighHighHigh
End of lifeRecyclable in principle, hard once dirtyHard to recycleHard to recycle

The biggest environmental win of any liner is the water it saves. Water that seeps away has already been pumped, harvested or bought. A liner that lasts longer also means less material thrown away. Good installation and maintenance are therefore the most practical way to lower the impact.

What about an unlined clay dam? Where good clay is on site, it has the lowest material footprint. It loses more water and needs more upkeep. On sandy soil it is not an option. Read more in our guide to lining dams on sandy and clay soil.

Frequently asked questions

Is a plastic dam liner safe for livestock water?

Yes. HDPE and PVC dam liners are widely used for livestock and irrigation water. For drinking water for people, choose a liner certified for that use.

Which is better, HDPE or PVC dam liner?

Neither is better everywhere. HDPE suits large earth dams in full sun. PVC suits steel tanks, small ponds and complex shapes.

Can I buy a plastic dam liner and install it myself?

For small ponds, sometimes. Large dam liners need a prepared base, heavy handling and tested welds, which need specialist equipment.

Does a dam liner harm the soil under it?

The soil under a liner stays drier than under an unlined dam. That is the point of the liner. The bigger effects come from how the site is cleared and shaped, so keep disturbance to the area that is needed.

Choose the right dam lining

title: HDPE Dam Liners: What They Are, How Thick, and When to Use One
excerpt: A plain guide to HDPE dam liners: what the material is, common thicknesses, UV life, how seams are welded and tested, and when another liner fits better.
content:
What is an HDPE dam liner, and is it the right one for your dam? An HDPE dam liner is a thick, stiff plastic sheet that is welded together on site to make one watertight skin inside an earth dam. It is the usual choice for larger farm, mining and game dams that stand in full sun. This guide explains the material, the thickness, how long it lasts and when another liner is the better fit.

Quick answer: HDPE dam liners

QuestionShort answer
What is it?High-density polyethylene sheet, black, made for lining dams and ponds
Usual thickness1.0 mm or 1.5 mm for most farm dams. Thinner and thicker sheet exists.
Sun (UV)Made to lie in the sun. Carbon black in the plastic protects it.
How long it lastsTypically 20 to 30 years on a farm dam when installed well. Not a guarantee.
Best forEarth dams, mining and process ponds, large reservoirs

What is HDPE?

HDPE stands for high-density polyethylene. It is the same family of plastic used for many water pipes. For dams, it is made into wide rolls of sheet called geomembrane.

The sheet is black because it contains a small amount of carbon black, usually about 2 to 3% by weight. The carbon black blocks ultraviolet (UV) light from the sun. That is why HDPE can lie exposed on a dam slope for many years.

HDPE has no plasticisers, the softening chemicals found in some flexible plastics. It stays stable and resists most salts, acids and fertiliser residues found in farm and mine water.

How an HDPE liner sits in an earth dam

The liner covers the floor and both slopes in one continuous sheet. At the top of each bank, the edge is buried in an anchor trench. The trench holds the liner in place against wind and the weight of the water.

What lies under the liner matters as much as the liner. Stones, roots and clods can push through the sheet once the dam is full. Installers smooth and compact the base first. On rough or stony ground they lay a geotextile, a thick felt-like fabric, under the liner as a cushion.

How thick should an HDPE dam liner be?

Thicker sheet is stronger and resists punctures better, but it costs more and is harder to fold into corners. The right thickness depends on the dam, not on a rule of thumb.

ThicknessWhere it is often used
0.75 mmSmall ponds and light-duty work on a well-prepared base
1.0 mmMany farm and irrigation dams on good ground
1.5 mmLarger or deeper dams, rougher ground, livestock nearby
2.0 mmMining and industrial ponds, heavy-duty work

We confirm the thickness after looking at the dam size, depth, slopes and ground. You can enter a preferred thickness in our dam lining calculator for a first estimate.

How are HDPE liner seams welded?

HDPE rolls are a few metres wide, so a dam liner is many sheets joined together. The joints are heat-welded on site, not glued. Most long seams are made with a wedge welder that fuses two strips at once.

The gap between the two welds is the test channel. The welder seals the ends, pumps in air and watches the pressure. If the pressure holds, the seam is tight. Patches and details round pipes are made with a hand extrusion welder and checked separately.

Good welding is the difference between a liner that holds water and one that leaks from day one. It needs the right machine, clean dry sheet and an experienced operator.

How long does an HDPE dam liner last?

A correctly installed, UV-stabilised HDPE liner typically lasts 20 to 30 years on a farm dam. That is a typical range, not a promise. What shortens it:

  • A poor base: stones and roots under the sheet.
  • Weak welds: seams that were not tested.
  • Stress: sheet pulled tight with no slack. HDPE grows and shrinks with heat, so installers leave some slack.
  • Damage: livestock, machinery and fallen branches.
  • Loose edges: a shallow anchor trench lets wind lift the liner.

Our guide to farm dam maintenance shows how to catch these problems early.

HDPE, PVC or bitumen: which liner fits?

LinerGood atUsual use
HDPESun, chemicals, large areasEarth dams, mining ponds
PVCFlexible, folds into shapesSteel tanks, small ponds
Bitumen torch-onBonds to a hard surfaceConcrete and masonry dams

PVC is easier to fit into a round steel tank or a pond with many corners. Bitumen suits rigid dams where the membrane must stick to the concrete. Read our comparison of HDPE, PVC and bitumen dam liners for more detail.

Frequently asked questions

What thickness HDPE liner do I need for a farm dam?

Most farm dams use 1.0 mm or 1.5 mm HDPE. Larger, deeper dams and rougher ground need the thicker sheet. We confirm it on site.

Are HDPE dam liners UV resistant?

Yes. Dam-grade HDPE contains carbon black and stabilisers so it can lie exposed in full sun for many years.

Can an HDPE liner go into an existing earth dam?

Yes, once the dam is drained and dry enough to work in. The base is cleared, shaped and smoothed before the liner goes in.

Can a damaged HDPE liner be repaired?

Yes. Holes and tears are cleaned and covered with an HDPE patch that is extrusion-welded in place. See our dam repair service.
